title: About US Quakes
intro: This map is not an earthquake or tsunami warning service. This copy is only as new as its last refresh, shown on the Live sheet. It draws the U.S. Geological Survey’s catalog of earthquakes in four map boxes: the Lower 48, Alaska with the Aleutians, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico with the Virgin Islands. 385 071 earthquakes from 1638 to 2025 ship with the app; the last 30 days arrive with each refresh.

reading.title: Size
reading.text: Each whole step of magnitude doubles a dot’s area, down to magnitude 2.2; smaller earthquakes share the smallest dot. It is a display rule, not a measure of energy.

reading.title: Color
reading.text: Color is depth as the catalog gives it: straw near the surface, then amber, rose, mauve and violet, to slate navy at 300 km and deeper. The stops sit at 0, 10, 35, 70, 150 and 300 km.

reading.title: Hollow
reading.text: A hollow ring is an automatic solution from the last 30 days that no person has reviewed yet; it may move, change size or disappear. A ring is never drawn smaller than a magnitude 4 dot, so that its hole shows. Older rows the catalog still lists as automatic are drawn solid, and their card says so.

reading.title: Gray
reading.text: A gray dot has no depth in the catalog: 1 492 rows in the history, 607 of them before 1900.
A small × has no magnitude: 180 rows, every one before 1900. They are drawn only while the window reaches back before 1900.

reading.title: Fade
reading.text: Within a window, older dots are paler; in All, every dot is drawn at the same half strength. The paleness is a display choice, not a measurement.

reading.title: Display choices
reading.text: These are presentation, not data: the color ramp and its stops; the thin rim around each dot, dark above 60 km and light from 60 km down; the fading of older dots; the faint trace Play leaves; the dimming outside a cross-section; the shaded relief, its level stretch and its strength; the tints of the sea; the hatching where the map ends; and the ink of the record strip, whose density counts events.

notes.title: Not a warning service
notes.text: This map is not an earthquake or tsunami warning service. This copy is only as new as its last refresh, shown on the Live sheet.

notes.title: More dots mostly means more seismometers
notes.text: The history holds 7 712 earthquakes before 1950 and 253 778 from 2000 on. Most of that rise is in the instruments, not in the Earth.
notes.quote: The ComCat earthquake catalog contains an increasing number of earthquakes in recent years--not because there are more earthquakes, but because there are more seismic instruments and they are able to record more earthquakes.

notes.title: What the catalog catches
notes.text: From 1900 this app keeps magnitude 2.5 and up; before 1900, every earthquake the catalog lists. Smaller earthquakes are missing unevenly from place to place.
notes.quote: For much of the U.S., earthquakes of magnitude 2.5 or larger are located and cataloged by the USGS/NEIC. In other parts of the U.S., the threshold of earthquakes that can be located and cataloged is higher, due either to the remoteness of those regions from seismographs or due to earthquake levels that are so high that a higher threshold of cataloging still reveals the important features of local seismicity. Within the conterminous U.S., the level of completeness for earthquake location by the USGS/NEIC is probably in the magnitude 3.0-3.5 range.

notes.title: Magnitude types differ
notes.text: Each event’s card shows the magnitude type the catalog gives (33 labels in the history), and none is converted into another.
notes.quote: Multiple methods are used to estimate magnitude. Fundamentally different calculation methods are specified by magnitude type.

notes.title: Automatic solutions change or vanish
notes.text: A live earthquake marked automatic has not been checked by a person yet. Its place, depth or size may change, and it may be deleted.
notes.quote: The faster we release earthquake locations and magnitudes, the more likely it is that the information may be erroneous.

notes.title: A depth of 10 km is often assigned
notes.text: 23 759 earthquakes in the history sit at exactly 10 km. That depth can be one assigned when the data could not fix one, and such rows line up flat in a cross-section.
notes.quote: Ten kilometers is a "fixed depth." Sometimes data are too poor to compute a reliable depth for an earthquake. In such cases, the depth is assigned to be 10 km.

notes.title: Negative depths
notes.text: 11 448 rows in the history have a negative depth. The map colors them as 0 km deep, and the cross-section plots them above its 0 km line.
notes.quote: A negative depth can sometimes be an artifact of the poor resolution for a shallow event. … When the earthquake depth is very shallow, it can be reported as a negative depth.

notes.title: Mercator inflates the north
notes.text: At 61° N a kilometer is drawn 1.6 times as long as at 40° N, so an area there looks 2.5 times as large. The scale bar is measured at the latitude of the map’s center.

notes.title: Boxes, not borders
notes.text: The four map boxes also take in earthquakes outside the United States, among them in Canada, Mexico, Russia and the Dominican Republic, and the app shows them as they are. Counts are labeled by map box, never by state or country.

notes.title: Before 1900, nominal
notes.text: The catalog lists 625 earthquakes from 1638 to 1899, 607 of them without a depth. Their times and positions are as the catalog lists them, often round numbers; the 1700 Cascadia earthquake is a single point.

notes.title: The history is a snapshot
notes.text: Rows are as USGS listed them when retrieved on 2026-09-30. Later revisions arrive only with a new copy of the app.

notes.title: Only earthquakes
notes.text: 12 942 other events in the catalog are left out, among them 673 nuclear explosions, 3 224 quarry blasts and 5 679 explosions.

notes.title: Faults are not a hazard map
notes.text: The fault lines are the Quaternary Fault and Fold Database: evidence of movement in the geological past, not a rating of danger. Nearness is not cause: a dot beside a fault does not say that fault moved.
notes.quote: This database contains information on faults and associated folds in the United States that demonstrate geological evidence of coseismic surface deformation in large earthquakes during the past 1.6 million years (Ma).

notes.title: Not monitored is not Normal
notes.text: A volcano the USGS does not list as monitored has no alert level. The map draws it empty and calls it not monitored, never Normal.

notes.title: Shaded relief
notes.text: Relief is drawn wherever the 3DEP elevation service had data: the United States and, near its borders, parts of Canada and Mexico; the Bahamas have none. The shading, its level stretch and its strength are display choices.

notShown.title: What this app does not show, and why
notShown.text: No globe and no worldwide catalog: the story here is the United States. No hazard model: a model is not a measurement. No ShakeMap or Did You Feel It? maps: they are separate USGS products; the felt count is shown. No Guam, Northern Marianas or American Samoa: they are outside the four map boxes. No explosions, quarry blasts or nuclear tests: they are not earthquakes. No heat maps, clustering or interpolated rates: each would draw something the catalog does not hold. No links: the app has no network.

status.label: Reviewed or automatic
status.quote: Status is either automatic or reviewed. Automatic events are directly posted by automatic processing systems and have not been verified or altered by a human. Reviewed events have been looked at by a human.

felt.label: Felt reports
felt.quote: The total number of felt reports submitted to the DYFI? system.

more.quote: Did You Feel It? (DYFI) collects information from people who felt an earthquake and creates maps that show what people experienced and the extent of damage.

tsunami.label: Tsunami flag
tsunami.quote: This flag is set to "1" for large events in oceanic regions and "0" otherwise. The existence or value of this flag does not indicate if a tsunami actually did or will exist.

alert.label: PAGER alert
alert.quote: The alert level from the PAGER earthquake impact scale.

more.quote: The PAGER system provides fatality and economic loss impact estimates following significant earthquakes worldwide.

sig.label: Significance
sig.quote: A number describing how significant the event is. Larger numbers indicate a more significant event.

magType.label: Magnitude type
magType.quote: The method or algorithm used to calculate the preferred magnitude for the event.

depth.label: Depth
depth.quote: This depth may be relative to the WGS84 geoid, mean sea-level, or the average elevation of the seismic stations which provided arrival-time data for the earthquake location.

fixedDepth.label: Fixed depth
fixedDepth.quote: Sometimes when depth is poorly constrained by available seismic data, the location program will set the depth at a fixed value.

more.quote: Ten kilometers is a "fixed depth." Sometimes data are too poor to compute a reliable depth for an earthquake. In such cases, the depth is assigned to be 10 km.

mww.name: moment, W-phase
mww.quote: Derived from a centroid moment tensor inversion of the W-phase

mwc.name: moment, centroid
mwc.quote: Derived from a centroid moment tensor inversion of the long-period surface waves

mwb.name: moment, body wave
mwb.quote: Derived from moment tensor inversion of long-period (~20-200 s; pass band based on size of EQ) body-waves (P- and SH).

mwr.name: moment, regional
mwr.quote: Based on the scalar seismic-moment of the earthquake, derived from moment tensor inversion of the whole seismogram at regional distances

ms.name: surface wave
ms.quote: A magnitude based on the amplitude of Rayleigh surface waves measured at a period near 20 sec.

mb.name: short-period body wave
mb.quote: Based on the amplitude of 1st arriving P-waves at periods of about 1 s.

mfa.name: felt area
mfa.quote: An estimate of body-wave (mb) magnitude based on the size of the area over which the earthquake was felt

ml.name: local
ml.quote: The original magnitude relationship defined by Richter and Gutenberg in 1935 for local earthquakes.

mb_lg.name: short-period surface wave
mb_lg.header: mb_Lg, mb_lg, or MLg (short-period surface wave)
mb_lg.quote: A magnitude for regional earthquakes based on the amplitude of the Lg surface waves as recorded on short-period instruments.

mlg.name: short-period surface wave
mlg.header: mb_Lg, mb_lg, or MLg (short-period surface wave)
mlg.quote: A magnitude for regional earthquakes based on the amplitude of the Lg surface waves as recorded on short-period instruments.

md.name: duration
md.quote: Based on the duration of shaking as measured by the time decay of the amplitude of the seismogram.

mwp.name: integrated P-wave
mwp.quote: Based on an estimate of moment calculated from the integral of the displacement of the P wave recorded on broadband instruments.

mh.name: non-standard method
mh.quote: Non-standard magnitude method. Generally used when standard methods will not work.

mint.name: intensity
mint.quote: A magnitude estimated from the maximum reported intensity, typically for earthquakes occurring before seismic instruments were in general use.

magTypeRule: Labels are matched without regard to case (Md and md, Ml and ml, Mb and mb, Mfa and mfa, Mw and mw). A label the USGS table does not name (for example mc, mlv, mblg) is shown as its code only.

faultScope.quote: This database contains information on faults and associated folds in the United States that demonstrate geological evidence of coseismic surface deformation in large earthquakes during the past 1.6 million years (Ma).

faultAgesNote: No USGS page read for this build states the time bounds of the database’s age classes, so the app prints the class names only.

A.quote: Geologic evidence demonstrates the existence of a Quaternary fault of tectonic origin, whether the fault is exposed for mapping or inferred from liquefaction or other deformational features.

B.quote: Geologic evidence demonstrates the existence of a fault or suggests Quaternary deformation, but either (1) the fault might not extend deeply enough to be a potential source of significant earthquakes, or (2) the currently available geologic evidence is too strong to confidently assign the feature to Class C but not strong enough to assign it to Class A.

C.quote: Geologic evidence is insufficient to demonstrate (1) the existence of tectonic fault, or (2) Quaternary slip or deformation associated with the feature.

NORMAL.quote: Volcano is in typical background, noneruptive state or, after a change from a higher level, volcanic activity has ceased and volcano has returned to noneruptive background state.

ADVISORY.quote: Volcano is exhibiting signs of elevated unrest above known background level or, after a change from a higher level, volcanic activity has decreased significantly but continues to be closely monitored for possible renewed increase.

WATCH.quote: Volcano is exhibiting heightened or escalating unrest with increased potential of eruption, timeframe uncertain, OR eruption is underway but poses limited hazards.

WARNING.quote: Hazardous eruption is imminent, underway, or suspected.

GREEN.quote: Volcano is in typical background, non-eruptive state or, after a change from a higher level, volcanic activity has ceased and volcano has returned to noneruptive background state.

YELLOW.quote: Volcano is exhibiting signs of elevated unrest above known background level or, after a change from a higher level, volcanic activity has decreased significantly but continues to be closely monitored for possible renewed increase.

ORANGE.quote: Volcano is exhibiting heightened or escalating unrest with increased potential of eruption, timeframe uncertain, OR eruption is underway with no or minor volcanic-ash emissions [ash- plume height specified, if possible].

RED.quote: Eruption is imminent with significant emission of volcanic ash into the atmosphere likely OR eruption is underway or suspected with significant emission of volcanic ash into the atmosphere [ash-plume height specified, if possible].

eventPageEvidence: USGS’s own record of ci38457511 (the event service’s GeoJSON) gives its url as earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/eventpage/ci38457511, and that address answered HTTP 200 on 2026-09-30.
